narrative: During the 1940s, Black and African women's hairstyles and hair culture were deeply rooted in tradition and community. While specific details about hairstyles during this decade are limited within the source material, we can infer that cornrows and other forms of braiding were likely popularized as a way to maintain and adorn their natural hair textures. The afro, which emerged later in the 1960s, was not yet a defining feature of Black beauty standards. Instead, women may have employed protective hairstyles such as Bantu knots or box braids to care for their hair while also expressing their cultural heritage. As African-American culture and identity continued to evolve during this period, hairstyles played an integral role in self-expression and community connection.
